memory_update.text: Coherent and Lumentum are the main reference public comps for direct InP/photonics capacity exposure in this node.

Aeluma is a speculative underfollowed alternative-photonics candidate because its III-V-on-silicon positioning could reduce dependence on native InP substrate capacity if commercialization proves real.
Need a later pass focused on pure-play optical engine, CPO, and substrate/equipment suppliers to fill the underfollowed lane beyond the obvious optical-component leaders.
LITE should be retained as a reference anchor for InP laser/device scarcity, not as the main underfollowed alpha lane.

ALMU is a speculative shadow-lane candidate for alternative III-V-on-silicon photodetectors and InP-on-silicon scaling; survival depends on customer qualification, production yield, and material revenue evidence.
POET is a speculative shadow-lane optical-engine and external-light-source integration candidate; track whether partnerships convert into production orders and recurring shipments.
FN is a second-order manufacturing-capacity candidate for optical communications/datacom/DCI ramps; verify AI-specific exposure versus broader telecom/datacom cyclicality.
The node appears to split into three research subnodes: native InP device capacity, alternative III-V-on-silicon platforms, and optical-engine/module assembly capacity.

Need a follow-up search for US-listed or ADR-accessible upstream equipment/materials tied to InP epitaxy, MOCVD, bonding, inspection, and wafer-level photonics test; many likely chokepoint suppliers may be non-US-listed.
COHR should remain the reference anchor for AI optical-capacity research because it discloses AI/ML transceivers, InP lasers, detectors, silicon photonics, and CPO-enabling technologies.

AXTI is a priority underfollowed substrate candidate for the InP chokepoint, but the thesis requires verification of AI-datacenter-linked backlog, material mix, customer concentration, and geopolitical operating risk.
FN is a second-order optical packaging, assembly, and test candidate; its chokepoint role depends on whether datacom/datacenter-interconnect growth is tied to 800G/1.6T AI optics.

ALMU belongs in the speculative shadow lane as a small-cap alternative photonics platform; it should not survive later layers without customer qualification, production-yield, and commercial-revenue evidence.

Future passes should test whether receive-side photodetectors, optical packaging/test capacity, and InP substrate supply are being priced less efficiently than lasers and finished transceiver vendors.
COHR should remain a reference anchor for InP/compound-semiconductor optical capacity, but not the primary underfollowed alpha lane due to high attention and large-cap status.
ALMU is a speculative-shadow candidate for alternative III-V-on-silicon photonics; survival to later layers requires customer qualification, commercial revenue, and wafer-yield evidence.
AAOI has direct AI datacenter optical-transceiver order evidence and should be checked for customer concentration, margin conversion, and dependence on constrained optical components.
Fabrinet maps to the manufacturing-capacity layer of AI optical interconnects, not the InP wafer/device layer; it may benefit if OEMs outsource 800G/1.6T scale-up.

Need a focused follow-up search for pure-play US-listed photodetector, InP substrate, MOCVD/etch/bonding equipment, and optical-engine names; POET and other micro/small caps require stronger primary-source verification before inclusion.

node: InP wafers, photodetectors, lasers, optical engines, and alternative photonics platforms
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Direct public-company exposure to the InP / photonics capacity node is concentrated in a small set of obvious leaders plus a narrower underfollowed lane. The strongest reference names are the established optical-component vendors with direct InP dependency and the hyperscaler/customer anchor NVIDIA. The underfollowed discovery lane is led by alternative integration platforms that may reduce dependence on native InP substrate capacity, but these remain hypothesis-level until commercial volume, customer wins, or signed capacity agreements are verified. Overall, the most important research question is whether hyperscaler pre-buying and AI optics demand are creating a durable capacity bottleneck in InP-based devices and whether alternative silicon-based photonics can scale fast enough to matter. Layer 1B expands the public universe around the AI optical-capacity chokepoint. The strongest reference evidence points to InP laser and optical-component capacity becoming strategically scarce as AI data-center bandwidth demand shifts toward 800G, 1.6T, external laser sources, silicon photonics, and co-packaged or near-packaged optics. The discovery lane should not stop at obvious optical-component leaders; it should track alternative III-V-on-silicon platforms, optical-engine integrators, and outsourced precision manufacturing capacity that may benefit if hyperscalers pre-buy scarce photonics supply.
